summary_md:
Dai et al. (Neural Networks 183, 2025) propose FOLAR, a stance detector with three parts. First, chain-of-thought prompts ask an LLM to write a first-order-logic (FOL) rule for each text and target. Second, a logic tensor network (LTN) uses a shared BERT and soft operators (negation 1-U, product conjunction, implication 1-U1+U1U2) to turn the rule into a differentiable classifier. Third, the LTNs built from GPT-3.5, Claude-2 and LLaMA-2 are fused by attention routing. The tests use English political tweets (SemEval-2016, ISD) and VAST. On in-target SEM16 and ISD the gains are small: +1.7 F_avg on LA and +2.0 on DT_I, and FOLAR is not the best on FM or HC. Zero-shot VAST gains are larger: +4.2 with full training data and +6.2 with 10% of it. The fusion ablation is about 5.8 points, but it compares fusion with a single GPT-3.5 model, so fusion is not separated from the choice of LLM. The paper reports no standard deviations, does not name its significance test, and its tables contain internal inconsistencies. The interpretability claim rests only on a 100-item, 3-rater check.

For Paul's system, the paper matters most as a formal version of something already built. The two-hop CU-alignment rule in fec/stance/apply_two_hop_stance.py composes stance with valence by hard sign multiplication over a hand-curated registry. FOLAR is the soft, learned, LLM-elicited form of that rule. It also gives a candidate route for the registry-coverage problem, but its error analysis (the LLM linking unrelated positive words to the target) names the same failure that sank the system's automatic-registry variants. The fusion result points to a cheap check on single-labeller bias in the Claude pre-labels that the DEBATE reader distils. It does not show that switching to FOLAR would beat a fine-tuned DEBATE or SVM on 87 to 156 held-out CU press items. The domain, the text genre and the LLM versions all differ.

bearings.paper_claim: FOL rules elicited from an LLM (Table 5 bike-lane rule links congestion to Against) are made differentiable with soft-logic operators: negation 1-U, conjunction U1*U2, implication 1-U1+U1*U2 (Eqs 2-5), and trained end to end with cross-entropy (Eq 12). Zero-shot VAST all-class F_avg: 81.0 vs 76.8 for KASD with 100 percent training data (+4.2); 80.2 vs 74.0 for MPPT with 10 percent (+6.2). Error analysis of 50 VAST errors (Sec 4.8) names LLM over-inference that links a positive clause to the target, and clause-level polarity conflicts.
bearings.paper_location: Sec 3.1-3.2, Eqs 2-6; Table 4 (VAST columns); Table 5; Sec 4.8 and Table 6
bearings.system_side: compose() in apply_two_hop_stance.py is a hard sign flip: support with positive valence stays support, and the reverse flips; neutral and unrelated pass through. lookup() takes the first registry entry whose match substring appears in target plus text, and the flat model alignment is the fallback on a miss (line 55). The file docstring reports stance-hop 0.915, valence-hop 0.689 and oracle ceiling 0.872, and the eval prints a flat baseline of 0.677. The composed 0.782 and F1 0.754 and the claim that every automatic-registry variant fell below the flat baseline are not in the cited code.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Transfer is limited to the decomposition idea. FOLAR targets are benchmark targets, whereas the valence hop needs CU-specific, owner-judged knowledge that LLM priors do not supply. The paper's over-inference failure matches the automatic-registry failure in the system. LLM-elicited valence rules stay UNVERIFIED (DE-062) until scored against the 400 tweet golds under single-look rules. The paper gives no evidence that a soft operator beats an exact registry lookup where the registry has coverage.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper side holds: the equations, the 81.0 vs 76.8 and 80.2 vs 74.0 comparisons and the error analysis all check against Tables 4 and 6 and Sec 4.8. The paper example is a bike-lane rule rather than a general negative-consequence rule, so the paraphrase is loosened. Code side holds for the hard sign flip and substring lookup with fallback. The 0.782 and 0.754 composed scores and the all-variants-below-baseline claim are not in the cited file, so the system side is trimmed to what the code and its docstring show.

summary_issues: summary_md says the fusion result points to a check on the Claude pre-labels that the DEBATE reader distils. The cited stage5_debate.py is zero-shot NLI with no training, so distillation is not shown. The 'fine-tuned on 552 labels' and 87.2 percent claims in bearing 2 are not in the cited files.

summary_md cites 87 to 156 held-out CU press items. The 87 appears only in the bearing 3 system_side, which does not match train_tweet_stance.py (5-fold CV, no untouched split). The 156 appears in no cited file.

The composed two-hop score 0.782 / F1 0.754 and the claim that every automatic-registry variant fell below the flat baseline are not in apply_two_hop_stance.py. The 0.915, 0.689, 0.677 and 0.872 figures are in the file docstring or eval output.

Pre-labeller identity is inconsistent across system files: claude_stance.py defaults to claude-sonnet-4-6, train_tweet_stance.py calls its api labels Opus prelabel, and its docstring cites Fable API labels. The single Claude rater claim needs the model and version named.
summary_md and bearing 2 describe the benchmarks as 2016-2020 tweets. The paper gives no collection dates, calls only SEM16 and ISD inputs tweets, and does not describe VAST's source text.

Paul-alignment statements are unverified: the item has no paul_entries, so Paul's notes (stale, Birkenmaier endorsement) cannot be checked. The claim that the system already records the stance-times-valence rule in a registry is consistent with apply_two_hop_stance.py.

Related link zhou-2026-measuring-stance-dynamics is said to come from the same journal, but its item lists Information Processing and Management. The Kim 96.9 percent figure covers only the 391 items both coders agreed, not all items.

Extraction errors (ext, not rel) to fix before reuse: zero-shot SEM16 best competitors are wrong. MPPT HC 83.6 beats Ts-CoT 83.2; COLA LA 71.0 beats MPPT 70.1; COLA DT 71.2 beats FOLAR DT 70.9, so FOLAR does not win zero-shot DT. The 85.5 HC value is the w/o MDF row, not FOL-CoT, whose HC is 83.6.
Kappa: the paper reports kappa scores above 70 percent with an average of 76 percent, with the variant unnamed. Writing kappa about 0.76 in gaps_exposed misstates the paper's reporting.
The retirement of gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 and Claude-2 snapshots is not stated in the paper and was not checked here, so treat it as unverified.

The paper's interpretability claim is asserted, not tested. The only check is 100 items rated by three raters, plus qualitative Table 5 examples. Both the summary and the flags say this correctly; no change needed.

Coverage: all 3 bearings and all 5 related links were re-checked against the text and the cited code. Not covered: the 552-label set, the 87.2 percent agreement, the n=87 and 156 counts, and Paul's annotations, none of which appear in the cited files.
gaps_exposed: The valence hop has no soft or probabilistic form: compose() is hard sign multiplication, so valence confidence and partial registry matches are discarded (apply_two_hop_stance.py:27-33).

The pre-labels come from a single LLM (Claude). No second or third LLM rater exists to measure labeller-specific bias before human override, which bears on the open question of how much DEBATE accuracy is LLM agreement.

Claude's reason field is captured (claude_stance.py:93) but is never checked for quality. The paper at least rates rationales for salience, non-redundancy and non-contradiction (n=100, kappa about 0.76).
No low-data or new-target evaluation condition exists for CU stance. The paper shows that method rankings differ most in that condition.
flags: Nothing here conflicts with the SNA wording rules (D-025, D-021, the rejected cosponsorship and normalization proposals). The paper is pure text classification.

Any LLM-elicited FOL rules or valence links adopted from this method are new agent analysis and stay UNVERIFIED until a second path (human gold) reproduces them (DE-062). The paper's own error analysis shows LLM over-inference on target links, the same failure that made the automatic-registry variants fall below the flat baseline.

The paper's quality is weak for adoption. It reports no SDs or CIs over three runs and does not name its significance test. FOL-CoT shows the same 79.8 in both VAST rows (a likely copy error). The ISD counts disagree (6,027 in the text vs 5,588 in the table), and the SEM16 target exclusions are inconsistent. Data are 'available on request', and the gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 and Claude-2 snapshots are retired, so the results cannot be reproduced.
The interpretability claim is asserted, not tested. Do not quote FOLAR rationales as explanations of stance without a separate validation.
paul_alignment: The paper agrees with Paul's endorsement of LLM-based position extraction (Kim J. 2025, Birkenmaier). It also confirms the weakness he flagged, disentangling ambiguous statements: implicit or sarcastic stance and clause-level polarity conflicts are FOLAR's two named failure types. On the two-hop component, the paper's FOL implication operator is a formal answer to his question of how agreement is quantified when actors relate through a third party. The system already answers that question with the stance-times-valence registry, which his notes do not yet record. His notes are stale on that point, not this paper's. Paul has no annotation of Dai et al. The paper does not support replacing the SVM or DEBATE readers, which goes further than his view that bag-of-words baselines are outdated: FOLAR's in-target gains are small, and no SVM baseline was run.

related.why: Same task (stance in political tweets), comparing fine-tuned RoBERTa with traditional ML. Its title supports the framing as a source of the SVM and PLM comparison Dai omits; the full paper was not checked for those numbers.

A direction-aware lexicon addresses clause-level polarity direction, one of FOLAR's two named error types. The claim that the system rejected a whole-text version in bill-sign handling was not checked against the repo.
General guidance on using LLMs to label political text. It bears on validating FOLAR-style LLM-elicited labels and rationales.

Zhou models stance dynamics over time with temporal graph neural networks in Information Processing and Management. The earlier note that it is from the same journal as Dai is wrong; Dai is in Neural Networks. Dai classifies static stance.

Both use LLMs to extract positions toward a named target. Kim reports 96.9 percent agreement with two human coders, but only on the 391 items both coders agreed. Dai reports no equivalent agreement for its stance outputs.

backlinks.why: Title matches a logic tensor network stance paper with LLM enhancement. The claim that it extends the in-context family Burnham benchmarks was not verified, so relation is softened from extends.
Paul's vault describes it as fusing three LLM decisions by attention routing for stance on VAST, not an NLI method. It is a possible comparator for the NLI reader, not the same method.

extraction.title: Zhan and Cai 2025 SN-LSGDM consensus with KNN imputation
extraction.venue: Expert Systems With Applications, vol. 263, article 125705 (online 10 Nov 2024)
extraction.document_type: Journal article (research article, methods/model paper with numerical illustration and simulation)
extraction.coverage: Full extracted text read in chunks, lines 0-3295 (pp. 1-20, including Table 1, Table 2, and the reference list). Nothing skipped. Figures 1-9 are text-extracted only (no images), so figure content is taken from the paper's prose descriptions, not read off plots. Metadata hint matched (authors, venue, year); DOI, volume and article number added. Paul's markup: none (no markup files were listed for this task), so paul_markup is empty. Lobbying, elections, persuasion/turnout, legislators, text measurement and path-finding are absent from the paper; networks (social trust networks) and allocation-like cost minimization are covered.
extraction.research_question: How to reach a consensus in large-scale group decision-making (LSGDM) with social networks (SN-LSGDM) when decision-makers (DMs) submit incomplete fuzzy preference relations (IFPRs), while minimizing unit adjustment cost (UAC) and keeping trust relations dynamic. Sub-questions: (a) estimate missing preference entries using K-nearest neighbours in the trust network; (b) cluster DMs into subgroups using trust, preference similarity and UAC; (c) run a two-stage (individual and subgroup) feedback consensus process based on three-way decision (TWD) with a cost-minimizing optimization step.
extraction.theory: Consensus reaching process (CRP) with soft consensus; minimum-adjustment-cost feedback (Ben-Arieh and Easton 2007; unit adjustment cost); social trust networks and fuzzy sociometry (Wasserman and Faust 1994; Dong et al. 2018); additive consistency of fuzzy preference relations (Tanino 1984; Xu et al. 2017); K-nearest neighbour estimation (Cover and Hart 1967); three-way decision (Yao 2010) mapping DMs into Pos, Bnd and Neg regions via a comprehensive adjustment priority (CAP) threshold. The paper argues trust should drive both imputation and adjustment; no formal theorem or convergence proof is given.
extraction.data: Illustrative case (Sec. 5.1, p.11): venture-capital diversified investment, 20 DMs (e1-e20), 5 alternatives (x1-x5: green logistics, ecological materials, digital economy, sustainable energy, machine learning). 20 incomplete 5x5 fuzzy preference matrices with 39 missing entries. Standardized evaluation matrices and trust network are taken from Gong et al. (2024) and are not reproduced; the paper points to a GitHub repository and says "Data will be made available on request" (p.19). UAC values for the 20 DMs were generated randomly by a program and are listed in Sec. 6.1.2 (p.14). No calendar period is stated. Simulation (Sec. 6.2, p.15-16): DM count 50 to 5000 in steps of 50, 5 alternatives, randomly generated data. Robustness test (Sec. 6.3, p.16): p in {20,40,60,80,100}, n in {4,6,8,10,12}, missing probability 0.1/0.2/0.3, 10 repetitions per cell, synthetic data.
extraction.method:
Four-part model. (1) Missing-value estimation (Sec. 3.1, Defs 3.1-3.6, Eqs 11-19): find K trusted neighbours with known entry; similarity sim_K (Eqs 12-13) and membership mu (Eq 14, mu = (t + sim)/(1 + sim)); normalize to weights (Eq 15); reliability r (Eq 16); impute f = sum of weights times neighbour values (Eqs 17-18), filling highest-reliability entries first and iterating to convergence. Complexity O(K^2 n p) (Remark 3.2). (2) Improved k-means on the trust network (Sec. 3.2, Defs 3.7-3.8, Eqs 20-30): trust influence Int(e_u) (Eq 20); adaptive k and initial centroids via a trust-discrepancy threshold (Eqs 21-23, Algorithm 1); distance = comprehensive difference combining (1 - mutual influence) and |UAC_u - UAC_v| / 2 (Eqs 24-29); iterate to SSE convergence (Algorithm 2, Eq 30). Complexity O(k n p^2) (Remark 3.5). (3) TWD consensus (Sec. 4.1, Def 4.1, Eqs 31-33): Pos = DMs with CD >= theta_ideal; CAP_r = beta(1 - UAC_r) + ((1-beta)/2) t_r + ((1-beta)/2)(1 - CD_r) (Eq 32); threshold CAP_lambda = CAP_min + lambda(CAP_max - CAP_min) (Eq 33); Neg if CAP >= CAP_lambda else Bnd. (4) Two-stage optimization (Sec. 4.2, Eqs 34-40): stage 1 minimizes sum of UAC_u times sum |h_ij - f_ij| over Neg DMs subject to Pos-based trust-weighted adjustment constraints, solved as a linear program (Python linprog); trust update t* = t^(1 - t) (Eqs 35-36, 39-40); stage 2 repeats with subgroups as units (Eq 38). Stop when group consensus degree (GCD) >= theta_ideal. Overall complexity stated as O(k n p^2) (Remark 4.2). Parameters: beta = 0.4, lambda = 0.5, theta_ideal = 0.92, K = 4 (Sec. 5.1, p.11).</method>
<parameter name="identification">None. This is a design-and-simulation paper with no causal identification strategy. Support comes from one worked numerical example (p.11-14), sensitivity sweeps over K and beta (Sec. 6.1, Figs 3-5, p.14-15), synthetic DM-scaling simulations (Figs 6-7, p.15-16), a missing-value robustness grid (Fig 8, p.16), and one quantitative comparison with method M1 (Fig 9, p.16).
extraction.scope: Population: group decision-making panels (expert/DM groups) with trust networks and incomplete fuzzy preference relations. Worked case: one venture-capital portfolio problem with 20 DMs and 5 alternatives. Simulated panels: 50 to 5000 DMs. No institution, country or era is studied; the paper argues applicability to emergency management, infrastructure engineering, government and industry (Sec. 4.1, p.10; Sec. 7, p.19) but tests none of these. Submission received 8 Aug 2024, accepted 3 Nov 2024. Relevance to networks: trust networks are central. Relevance to lobbying, elections, persuasion/turnout, legislators, text measurement and path-finding: none.

Trust is the only factor used to pull dissenting DMs toward the group; other factors (expertise, track record, social influence) are deferred (Sec. 7, p.18-19).
The worked example uses one case with 20 DMs and 5 alternatives; larger groups are only simulated with random data (Sec. 5.1 p.11; Sec. 6.2 p.15).

Parameters beta=0.4, lambda=0.5 and theta_ideal=0.92 are set by the authors' judgement; only K and beta are swept, and lambda and theta are not swept (Sec. 5.1, p.11; Sec. 6.1.2, p.15).

summary_md:
Zhan and Cai (ESWA 2025) propose a consensus procedure for large groups whose members state incomplete fuzzy preference matrices and are linked by a trust network. It has four parts. (1) Missing preference entries are filled from the K most trusted neighbours who have that entry. Each neighbour is weighted by trust and preference similarity, the most reliable gaps are filled first, and filling repeats until stable. (2) Members are clustered with an adaptive k-means whose distance combines trust and unit adjustment cost (UAC). (3) A three-way decision rule sorts members into Pos, Bnd and Neg regions. (4) A two-stage linear program makes the cheapest preference adjustments, first per member and then per subgroup, until group consensus reaches 0.92.

All evidence is either one worked case or synthetic. The case has 20 decision-makers and 5 alternatives; its UAC values are random, and its trust network and preference data come from an earlier paper and are not reproduced. Group consensus rises from 0.9117 to 0.9368 over 11 rounds. The imputation MSE of 0.09 to 0.13 is measured only on randomly generated matrices. The paper compares numerically against one method, in a figure only. There is no causal identification, no holdout and no proof that the procedure converges.

The paper models committee-style preference aggregation. It does not model lobbying, legislators or influence, so most of Paul's systems are unaffected. Its one useful contact is network-neighbour imputation. The paper's estimator weights neighbours by tie strength and similarity and orders fills by reliability. The system's stance-dynamics proposer takes a plain mean over binary cosponsor neighbours. The extension is only worth testing because that same component found co-movement null on cosponsor ties. That null undercuts the homophily premise this whole imputation family relies on, and the paper never tests the premise on real data. Its "trust" is an elicited trust score, not cosponsorship. Reading cosponsor weights as trust would break D-025.

bearings.paper_claim: Missing preference entries are imputed from the K=4 most trusted neighbours with a known value. Each weight blends trust and preference similarity (mu = (t + sim)/(1 + sim), then normalized), and entries are filled in order of reliability r and iterated to convergence. In the worked case f10_45 = 0.4033 comes from 4 neighbours weighted 0.2549/0.2507/0.2503/0.2440, the highest-reliability gap (r = 3.8683) of 39 missing entries. Imputation MSE stays at 0.09-0.13 across p in {20..100}, n in {4..12} and missing rates 0.1/0.2/0.3, on synthetic data only.
bearings.system_side: The silent-member proposer takes each member's cosponsor neighbours as an UNWEIGHTED binary adjacency set (edge weights are dropped when the Edges sheet is read). It averages the neighbours' tier scores per category, with no similarity weighting, no reliability ordering and no iteration. It proposes a cell only when there are at least 5 neighbours (SD_MINNB) and |est| >= 0.75 (SD_CONF). It checks sign agreement on cells whose stance is already known, with no party-only baseline, and outputs proposals only. The same script reports co-movement as null on cosponsor ties.
bearings.code_ref: fec/stance/stance_dynamics.py:89-93 (binary adj from cosponsor Edges); fec/stance/stance_dynamics.py:132-147 (MINNB 5, CONF 0.75, unweighted mean, proposal-only); fec/stance/stance_dynamics.py:94-110 (co-movement test)
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the mechanics carry over: neighbour weights from tie strength plus profile similarity, and filling the best-supported gaps first. The paper's evidence does not transfer. Its MSE comes from random synthetic matrices; its trust network is elicited trust among decision-makers, not cosponsorship; its alternatives are 5 investment options, not legislators' CU stance categories. Its homophily premise is assumed, never tested, while this system measured co-movement as null on cosponsor ties. A weighted variant should be adopted only if a masked-cell test beats both the current unweighted mean and a party-only baseline on held-out members. Until a second path reproduces that result it stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062). Weights must be labelled heuristic tie strength, never trust or closeness (D-025).

gaps_exposed: The stance-dynamics masking check has no party-only baseline. Neither does the paper's MSE test. Neither can show that network-neighbour imputation adds anything beyond party (this is also the open question listed for the component).

The neighbour imputation ignores tie strength and similarity: binary adjacency gives weak and strong cosponsor ties equal votes. If imputation is kept at all, a weighted or reliability-ordered variant is the untested alternative.
Minor code-label mismatch: the summary print at fec/stance/stance_dynamics.py:152 says '>=3 informative neighbors', but the gate MINNB defaults to 5 (line 132).
flags: The paper's 'trust' is an elicited trust degree between decision-makers. Porting its weighting onto cosponsor or staffer edges and calling it trust would break D-025: graph weights are heuristic model outputs, never closeness, access or introduction probabilities.

The paper's KNN imputation assumes preferences are similar among network neighbours, but the system measured cosponsor-tie co-movement as null. Treat any claim that this paper supports neighbour imputation as unsupported for this corpus.

This paper argues for neither rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization). It does not use LDA. It reports a reciprocity-like 'mutual influence' term only inside clustering, which gives no support to reciprocity (D-104..D-108 status unchanged).
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotation of this paper. For the closest component (stance-dynamics), his note asks for temporal dynamics and change-likelihood modelling, and it predates the null co-movement result. This paper does not resolve that tension. Its neighbour-imputation evidence is synthetic and rests on an assumed homophily the system did not find. His note is stale on that point; nothing in this paper revives the premise.

related.why: The system's stance-dynamics imputer cites Zhou-Elejalde silent-actor collaborative filtering as its template (fec/stance/stance_dynamics.py:147). Zhan-Cai gives a trust- and similarity-weighted alternative to the same neighbour-imputation idea.
Cao 2025 is a survey of social-network group decision making, the field this paper belongs to. It places the paper's trust-driven consensus and minimum-cost feedback among related designs.
